title: In 1943 a volcano was born in a Mexican cornfield and grew 50 m in a day
body: On the afternoon of 20 February 1943, the ground opened in a cornfield owned by the farmer Dionisio Pulido, near the village of Parícutin in western Mexico, and began throwing out ash and rock. Within 24 hours a cone of cinders stood about **50 m** high. The new volcano kept erupting until 1952, when its cone rose 424 m above the valley floor. Because it grew from nothing in plain view, volcanologists could document the entire life cycle of a volcano for the first time.

cover.alt: Parícutin erupting at night in 1943, a glowing fountain of lava and streaks of red-hot rock pouring down a dark cone

slides.heading: How fast the cone grew
slides.note: Height of the cinder cone above the valley floor

slides.prompt: Lava and ash buried two villages. How many people died directly from the eruption?
slides.detail: No one died directly from it, though three people were killed by lightning generated by the explosive eruptions.

slides.alt: The stone bell tower and front of a ruined church rising out of a field of black hardened lava, with a volcanic cone on the horizon
slides.caption: The church of San Juan Parangaricutiro, still poking out of the hardened lava. The village of Parícutin itself was completely covered.

slides.label: of land buried under lava
slides.text: Volcanic sand blanketed another 52 km², and the eruption damaged an area of about 233 km² in all.

slides.question: For how long did Parícutin keep erupting?
slides.explanation: It began in February 1943 and its last recorded burst came in early 1952. Cinder cones like this one usually go extinct once they have formed.
